l2: Not *obviously*. The evidence splits by setup: hybrid arrangements mostly show no drop in performance, while some fully remote studies do find real productivity losses. What holds up better is narrower — newer people tend to get less feedback and mentoring away from colleagues — so the claim you can defend depends on which teams and what kind of productivity you mean.
l3: That's one textbook model, not the whole of economics: the competitive case predicts job losses, but where employers have wage-setting power a moderate minimum can leave employment flat or even raise it, and the evidence since Card and Krueger's 1994 fast-food study is genuinely split. What does hold up is that size matters — a minimum close to the local median wage is far more likely to cost jobs than a modest one — so *always* is the word that fails.
l4: It turns on three things the money-versus-friends framing hides: what the raise actually buys once the new city's costs come out of it, which of these friendships would survive the distance rather than fade without proximity, and whether the job itself is a step forward or just better paid.
l5: It's the probability of a result at least as extreme as yours *if* the null hypothesis were true — $P(\text{data this extreme} \mid H_0)$, the share of the null distribution lying at least as far out as your test statistic. It is not the chance the null is true, $P(H_0 \mid \text{data})$: it tells you how surprising your data would be in a world where the null holds, not how likely that world is.
